title: Chemical Reactions and Equations
subject: Science

notes.heading: Chemical Reaction
notes.text: A chemical reaction is a process in which one or more substances change into new substances with different properties. The substances that take part in a chemical reaction are called reactants, and the new substances formed are called products.
points: A chemical reaction may be identified by:
notes.example: When magnesium burns in oxygen: Magnesium + Oxygen ⟶ Magnesium oxide. Here: Reactants = Magnesium + Oxygen; Product = Magnesium oxide.

notes.heading: Chemical Equation
notes.text: A chemical equation is a short representation of a chemical reaction using the symbols and chemical formulae of the substances involved.
points: Chemical Equation = Symbolic representation of the process

notes.heading: 1.1 Chemical Equations
notes.text: A chemical equation is a symbolic representation of a chemical reaction. Instead of writing the names of substances, we use their chemical symbols and formulae.
points: The reaction between hydrogen and oxygen to form water can be written as:
H₂ and O₂ are the reactants.
A chemical equation gives us information about which substances react and which substances are formed.
notes.example: The reaction between hydrogen and oxygen to form water can be written as: Hydrogen + Oxygen ⟶ Water. Using chemical formulae: H₂ + O₂ ⟶ H₂O.

notes.heading: 1.1.1 Writing a Chemical Equation
notes.text: A chemical equation represents a chemical reaction using the symbols and formulae of the substances involved.
points: Steps for writing a chemical equation
numberedPoints: Write the reactants on the left-hand side.
Write the products on the right-hand side.
Separate reactants and products using an arrow ⟶.
notes.example: When magnesium reacts with oxygen, magnesium oxide is formed. In words: Magnesium + Oxygen ⟶ Magnesium oxide. Using chemical formulae: Mg + O₂ ⟶ MgO. Here: Mg, O₂ = Reactants; MgO = Product.

notes.heading: Skeletal Chemical Equation
notes.text: This equation is called a skeletal chemical equation because it represents the reaction but is not balanced.
points: Remember: Reactants are written on the left-hand side, and products are written on the right-hand side.

notes.heading: 1.1.2 Balanced Chemical Equations
notes.text: A balanced chemical equation is an equation in which the number of atoms of each element is equal on both sides of the equation. This is based on the Law of Conservation of Mass, which states that mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.
points: The number of oxygen atoms is not equal, so the equation is not balanced.
We balance it by putting suitable numbers called coefficients before the formulae:
notes.example: Consider: Mg + O₂ ⟶ MgO. Count the atoms: Mg — Left side 1, Right side 1; O — Left side 2, Right side 1. We balance it by putting suitable numbers called coefficients before the formulae: 2Mg + O₂ ⟶ 2MgO. Now: Mg — Left side 2, Right side 2; O — Left side 2, Right side 2. Therefore, the equation is balanced.

notes.heading: Important Rule
notes.text: While balancing an equation, we change only the coefficients, not the chemical formulae.
points: But we should not change H₂O into another formula just to balance the equation.
Number of atoms of each element on LHS = Number of atoms on RHS
A balanced chemical equation obeys the law of conservation of mass.

notes.heading: 1.2 Types of Chemical Reactions
notes.text: Chemical reactions can be classified into different types depending on how the reactants change into products. The main types are:
points: These reactions have different patterns, which help us identify them easily.

notes.heading: 1.2.1 Combination Reaction
notes.text: A combination reaction is a reaction in which two or more substances combine to form a single product.
points: Here, two or more reactants combine to form only one product.
Calcium reacts with oxygen to form calcium oxide:
Here, calcium and oxygen combine to form one product, calcium oxide.
notes.example: Example 1: Formation of Calcium Oxide. Calcium reacts with oxygen to form calcium oxide: 2Ca + O₂ ⟶ 2CaO. Here, calcium and oxygen combine to form one product, calcium oxide.

notes.heading: Combination Reaction — Examples 2 and 3
notes.text: Again, two reactants combine to form one product.
points: Hydrogen reacts with oxygen to form water:
Carbon combines with oxygen to form carbon dioxide:
The easiest way to identify a combination reaction is:
Two or more reactants ⟶ One product
So, many substances combine to give one substance.
notes.example: Example 2: Formation of Water — Hydrogen reacts with oxygen to form water: 2H₂ + O₂ ⟶ 2H₂O. Example 3: Burning of Coal — Carbon combines with oxygen to form carbon dioxide: C + O₂ ⟶ CO₂.

notes.heading: 1.2.2 Decomposition Reaction
notes.text: A decomposition reaction is a reaction in which one compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances. It is the opposite of a combination reaction.
points: Here, one reactant breaks down to form two or more products.
On heating calcium carbonate, it decomposes into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide:
Water can be decomposed into hydrogen and oxygen by passing electricity through it:
notes.example: Example 1: Decomposition of Calcium Carbonate — On heating calcium carbonate, it decomposes into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide: CaCO₃ —Δ→ CaO + CO₂. Here, Δ represents heat. Example 2: Decomposition of Water — Water can be decomposed into hydrogen and oxygen by passing electricity through it: 2H₂O —electricity→ 2H₂ + O₂.

notes.heading: Types of Decomposition Reactions
notes.text: Decomposition can occur due to:
points: One reactant ⟶ Two or more products
So, in a decomposition reaction, one compound breaks down into simpler substances.

notes.heading: 1.2.3 Displacement Reaction
notes.text: A displacement reaction is a reaction in which a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its compound.
points: Here, element A is more reactive than B, so A displaces B from the compound BC.
Zinc reacts with copper sulphate solution:
Zinc (Zn) is more reactive than copper (Cu).
Zinc displaces copper from copper sulphate.
Zinc sulphate and copper are formed.
Iron displaces copper from copper sulphate:
More reactive element + Compound ⟶ New compound + Less reactive element
Remember: A displacement reaction involves the displacement of one element by another more reactive element.
notes.example: Zinc reacts with copper sulphate solution: Zn + CuSO₄ ⟶ ZnSO₄ + Cu. Another example: Iron displaces copper from copper sulphate: Fe + CuSO₄ ⟶ FeSO₄ + Cu.

notes.heading: 1.2.4 Double Displacement Reaction
notes.text: A double displacement reaction is a reaction in which two compounds exchange their ions to form two new compounds.
points: Here, the ions of the two compounds exchange places.
When sodium sulphate reacts with barium chloride:
Na₂SO₄ and BaCl₂ are the reactants.
BaSO₄ and NaCl are the products.
BaSO₄ is an insoluble white solid called a precipitate.
Therefore, this reaction is also called a precipitation reaction.
The compounds exchange their ions during the reaction.
notes.example: When sodium sulphate reacts with barium chloride: Na₂SO₄ + BaCl₂ ⟶ BaSO₄ + 2NaCl. BaSO₄ is an insoluble white solid called a precipitate.

notes.heading: Oxidation and Reduction
notes.text: Oxidation and reduction are chemical processes that often occur together in a reaction.

notes.heading: Oxidation
notes.text: Oxidation can be understood as:
points: Copper combines with oxygen, so copper is oxidised.

notes.heading: Reduction
notes.text: Reduction can be understood as:
points: Oxygen is removed from copper oxide, so copper oxide is reduced.

notes.heading: Oxidation and Reduction Together
notes.text: When oxidation and reduction occur in the same reaction, the reaction is called a redox reaction.
points: Thus, oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously.

notes.heading: 1.3 Effects of Oxidation Reactions in Everyday Life
notes.text: Oxidation reactions do not occur only in laboratories. They also happen around us in everyday life.
points: Two important effects of oxidation are:
These processes can cause damage to metals and food.

notes.heading: 1.3.1 Corrosion
notes.text: Corrosion is the process in which a metal is gradually destroyed or damaged due to reactions with substances present in the environment, such as oxygen, moisture, acids, etc.
points: Iron reacts with oxygen and moisture present in air to form rust.
Rust is mainly hydrated iron(III) oxide.
The reddish-brown coating seen on iron objects is rust.
Copper develops a green coating of basic copper carbonate.
Silver develops a black coating of silver sulphide.
Corrosion can be prevented by protecting the metal from contact with air and moisture.
Corrosion = Gradual damage of a metal due to environmental reactions
Rusting of iron is one of the most common examples of corrosion.
notes.example: Example: Rusting of Iron — Iron reacts with oxygen and moisture present in air to form rust. Iron + Oxygen + Water ⟶ Rust. Rust is mainly hydrated iron(III) oxide: Fe₂O₃ · xH₂O.

notes.heading: 1.3.2 Rancidity
notes.text: Rancidity is the process in which food containing fats and oils gets oxidised, causing an unpleasant smell and taste.
points: For example, when oily food is left exposed to air for a long time, it may develop a bad smell and taste. This happens because the fats and oils in the food undergo oxidation.
Rancidity can be prevented or slowed down by:
Keeping food in airtight containers to prevent contact with oxygen.
Refrigerating food, which slows down oxidation.
Packing some foods using nitrogen gas instead of oxygen.
Chips packets are often filled with nitrogen gas. Nitrogen prevents the oils in the chips from coming into contact with oxygen and becoming rancid.
Rancidity = Oxidation of fats and oils causing unpleasant smell and taste
notes.example: Chips packets are often filled with nitrogen gas. Nitrogen prevents the oils in the chips from coming into contact with oxygen and becoming rancid.

summary: Chapter 1 explains chemical reactions and their symbolic representation as chemical equations. It covers chemical reactions, reactants and products, chemical equations, skeletal equations, balanced chemical equations and the Law of Conservation of Mass. It then explains combination, decomposition, displacement and double displacement reactions. Oxidation and reduction are introduced and their simultaneous occurrence is described as a redox reaction. The chapter also explains the effects of oxidation in everyday life, namely corrosion and rancidity, along with common methods of preventing corrosion and slowing down rancidity.

qa.a: A chemical reaction is a process in which one or more substances change into new substances with different properties.
The substances that take part in a chemical reaction are called reactants, and the new substances formed are called products.

qa.q: By what changes may a chemical reaction be identified?
qa.a: A chemical reaction may be identified by change in colour, change in temperature, formation of a gas, formation of a precipitate, or change in physical state.
A chemical equation is a short representation of a chemical reaction using the symbols and chemical formulae of the substances involved.

qa.q: What is a skeletal chemical equation?
qa.a: A skeletal chemical equation represents the reaction but is not balanced.

qa.q: What is a balanced chemical equation?
qa.a: A balanced chemical equation is an equation in which the number of atoms of each element is equal on both sides of the equation.

qa.q: Which law is followed by a balanced chemical equation?
qa.a: A balanced chemical equation obeys the law of conservation of mass.

qa.q: What should be changed while balancing an equation?
qa.a: Only the coefficients should be changed, not the chemical formulae.
A combination reaction is a reaction in which two or more substances combine to form a single product.

qa.q: What is the general form of a combination reaction?
qa.a: A + B ⟶ AB
A decomposition reaction is a reaction in which one compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances.

qa.q: What are the types of decomposition mentioned in the chapter?
qa.a: Thermal decomposition, electrolytic decomposition and photolytic decomposition.
A displacement reaction is a reaction in which a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its compound.

qa.q: What is a double displacement reaction?
qa.a: A double displacement reaction is a reaction in which two compounds exchange their ions to form two new compounds.

qa.q: Why is the sodium sulphate and barium chloride reaction called a precipitation reaction?
qa.a: Because BaSO₄ is an insoluble white solid called a precipitate.
Oxidation can be understood as addition of oxygen, removal of hydrogen, or loss of electrons.
Reduction can be understood as removal of oxygen, addition of hydrogen, or gain of electrons.
When oxidation and reduction occur in the same reaction, the reaction is called a redox reaction.

qa.q: What are the two important effects of oxidation in everyday life?
qa.a: Corrosion and rancidity.
qa.section: 1.3 Effects of Oxidation Reactions in Everyday Life

qa.a: Corrosion is the process in which a metal is gradually destroyed or damaged due to reactions with substances present in the environment, such as oxygen, moisture, acids, etc.
Rust is mainly hydrated iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃ · xH₂O.
Corrosion can be prevented by protecting the metal from contact with air and moisture. Common methods include painting, oiling or greasing, galvanisation and alloying.
Rancidity is the process in which food containing fats and oils gets oxidised, causing an unpleasant smell and taste.

qa.q: How can rancidity be prevented or slowed down?
qa.a: By adding antioxidants to food, keeping food in airtight containers to prevent contact with oxygen, refrigerating food, and packing some foods using nitrogen gas instead of oxygen.

qa.q: Why are chips packets filled with nitrogen gas?
qa.a: Nitrogen prevents the oils in the chips from coming into contact with oxygen and becoming rancid.
